name: Colossus Fall
geological_features: A nitrogen-methane atmosphere creating blue-white cloud systems of staggering scale
Ice mountains reaching 25km altitude on a surface of frozen methane
Cryogenic river systems of liquid nitrogen carving valleys across the surface
specific_features: Ruins of what appears to be an enormous installation buried under kilometers of ice at the equator
resources: Nitrogen in liquid form for industrial use
description: Colossus Fall is an ice giant that defies easy categorization, too large for a terrestrial world but possessing a solid surface beneath its dense cryogenic atmosphere. The surface is a frozen landscape of methane ice sculpted by nitrogen rivers into valleys and canyons of alien beauty, the ice mountains rising from the plains like the bones of a world too cold to decay. The atmosphere presses down with a weight felt in every movement, thick with nitrogen and methane that swirl into cloud formations the size of continents.

The light that reaches the surface through the dense atmosphere is a dim blue-white, casting everything in the tones of a world seen through deep water. The nitrogen rivers flow with a viscosity that makes them appear slow until one realizes their scale, each river kilometers wide and flowing at speeds that would be torrential on a warmer world. The methane ice groans under temperature changes, creating a soundscape of deep cracks and resonant booms that carry for hundreds of kilometers.

The ruins buried at the equator were discovered by deep-penetrating radar on the third orbital survey. Geometric structures of enormous scale lie beneath two kilometers of accumulated ice, their composition a metallic alloy that does not match any natural formation process. The installation, if that is what it is, appears to have been deliberately buried or simply overwhelmed by ice accumulation over an immense timescale. No entrance or surface feature marks its location.

Excavation proposals have been submitted by seven different research institutions, but the scale of the undertaking, removing two kilometers of methane ice in a dense cryogenic atmosphere, has stalled every plan at the funding stage. The ruins predate the ice accumulation by an estimated four billion years, placing their construction at a time when the planet may have been warmer and its surface accessible. Whatever civilization built them did so on a scale that matches the world itself, and their absence raises questions no one has comfortably answered.
